title: What is your experience like using AI to program games?
author: Wolfu0
selftext: I'm a game artist and I don't have much time to learn how to program, but I wanted to have short games to put in my portfolio. I want to learn how to program, especially because it's necessary to correct errors in the AI code, but I don't know if it's a promising thing to program games using AI. What do you think about it? Have you tried it? Have you had success?

replies.author: constPxl
replies.body:
if you are making unity or godot games, youd need unity or godot install. Youd need to use the application. If youre making javascript games, you can use any text based code application, though certain app like vs code is preferrable

comments.author: Fluid_Cup8329
comments.body:
I only use ai to make textures, but I have experimented with getting Gemini 2.5 to code a basic game. I simply told it to make an html game based around Asteroids with vector graphics that progressively change colors. It pulled it off pretty much flawlessly. 

That's the extent of my experiments with vibe coding a game, but it was highly successful even with a really simple prompt.

comments.author: Individual_Record521
comments.body:
I've been using AI solely with no coating experience and the biggest problem that I'm finding using AI engines is the lack of memory. 


Usually starts off very smooth and actually pretty functional but after you get well on your way the memory starts to become a big issue The game starts to bog down the engine starts to get very confused and the files simply become too large to be worked on and you have to jump through loops to try to get it to work

replies.author: c126
replies.body: Yes, it’s great for bits of code but 1000 lines or so

replies.author: Individual_Record521
replies.body: Yeah sucks. Been trying to think of ways to compartmentalize the code and use groc or another engine to make this process a little bit smoother because there's really big potential here

replies.author: drizel
replies.body:
Ask it about entity, component, system (ECS)  
Keep everything as compartmentalized and modular as you can. The file count goes up, but sizes can be kept down. I used it to write a script to concatenate all the files together into a mega dump for Gemini in the browser app. 

Tell you are a noob and don't know the right questions to ask.   
That prompt alone can move mountains sometimes.

My biggest problem is figuring out what I want to build...

replies.author: Individual_Record521
replies.body: Thanks, have you tried the game jam route?

comments.author: Rawesoul
comments.body:
I tried Claude for my game on Unity. It was fine until it couldn't add one  feature on 1/3 game prototype without breaking the rest of code. When I start the refactoring, Claude broke everything and can't fix. 🤣 But when I switched to Gemini 2,5, I successfully refactor the code and fix issues.

Basically, AI are good for gamedev, but you still need to know your game engine, its features, useful assets and configuring

My recommended stack: 
- Unity, GameMaker (but not Godot, because AIs are not good in it for now) 

- Gemini 2,5 Pro (not Flash)

- VSCode / Sublime Text (haven't used Cursor, Windsurf and other useful IDE for AI, just because I prefer copy-paste from browser)

comments.author: Donkeytonk
comments.body: I started 5 years ago learning to program myself. After 3-4 years started integrating AI into programming, which sped up my learning. If you can’t program then use it to learn. If you can program, use it to program higher quality and faster. Don’t ever think it can do all the programming for you though

comments.author: kytheon
comments.body:
Coding is an iterative process. You make something, see if it works, then fix the issues.

If your code has an issue, you can ask AI to analyze the issues, and give it the specific error or describe the situation.

And yes, AI can fix wrong code it wrote itself.

Don't try to ask it to write an entire game in a single prompt. Make a basic game, then ask it to improve and change.

comments.author: CeruleanSpirit123

Well, the good news is that as much as you can use AI to make art, you can use AI to produce code too. I personally use Godot, it's one of the best Game Engine for simple games. It uses GD script for the game logic, it's similar to python.

[https://godotengine.org/download/windows/](https://godotengine.org/download/windows/)

My recommendation:

comments.body: It's good for debugging but not creating a whole game. It's good side tool but I've not met and AI that create a whole game without significant input and editing.

comments.author: Lyvanthian
comments.body:
From my experience, if you work at small enough a scale, i.e. not editing the entire script but instead work on a method by method basis, and have clear defined logic, it keeps up just fine. It also has a nifty little feedback loop whereby the more you learn and advance in programming the more you can bounce those ideas off the ai meaning you can always have a direct implementation case for whatever you're trying to learn. In a way, the smarter you get the smarter it gets relatively speaking.

Hope that helps, again just my experience, the direct implementation element is what helped me the most

comments.author: donuz
comments.body:
Gemini 2.5 pro is absurdly good for game developing, and I think there are not any other AI's that is close to its performance, including ChatGPT-o3. It works even if you have like 50 different scripts. As long as you check line-by-line what AI suggested, it is much faster than coding by yourself.

For Unity, you can take some Learning Pathway courses and then start coding with AI. Not ideal but you would continue learning with AI too.

comments.author: mikeriemer
comments.body:
I am the principal engineer at a sports application startup. I have 14 yrs experience across enterprise Web and game development, mostly sports applications using game engines and related technologies like Blender, Houdini, Substance, Maya, Max and Marmoset etc. I have experience delivering software using Unity, Unreal Engine 4 and 5. I don't contribute a lot on Reddit but after reading these responses I wanted to give you a clearer picture of how generative A.I. is both perceived in the corporate landscape and how it is currently utilized.  I do want to note I was "late to the party" on A.I. I was a denier about its capabilities and how pervasive it would be come.

". I want to learn how to program, especially because it's necessary to correct errors in the AI code, but I don't know if it's a promising thing to program games using AI. What do you think about it? Have you tried it? Have you had success?"   
  
   \- Everyday you don't spend learning A.I. tools is a day farther behind your peers you will fall. Almost every company has A.I. initiatives right now. The more A.I. platforms/tools that you can prompt correctly the more value employers will see.  
   \- Also, part of participation in any kind of team that delivers software you have to get comfortable at reading and giving feedback on other team member's output. This could be code, art, infrastructure and documentation. Its best to look at A.I. output as output from a junior team member. This will give you the correct context for the value it can deliver.   
   \- Every single piece of (corporate) software currently under development has a percentage of its engineering done by A.I.  
   \- On the project I am overseeing right now, there are five different A.I. platforms that we are currently using to produce value. I wasn't the leader that brought these tools in. They were more or less, hoisted on me.  
   \- The only reason A.I. has not 100% decimated software engineering is you still need mid-to-senior-level engineers to both architect and oversee the work output of various A.I tools. Especially, around application security.  
   \- In my opinion if I were to start developing an indie game using Unity, depending on the exact requirements I could conservatively say. I could offload 50 - 75% of the technical workload to A.I. platforms/tools. If it was using UE5 the percentage would be more like 40-60%. This is assuming AAA quality game art.  
   \- Be careful of people saying the output is not of quality. Like anything else, prompting A.I. to give you the output you require is a skill that takes a tremendous amount learning and perfecting to get it right. If you cannot get the correct output, it is most likely the user not the A.I. platform/tool. (of course there are cases but these are becoming more rare by the day)

These are just my opinions that are derived from my experiences. You may have different priorities, goals and talents, but I just wanted to provide you some insight that may possibly inform your future decisions based on a general sense of the place of A.I. in the corporate world.

replies.author: Quind1
replies.body:
Thanks for this insightful/informative comment. As a professional SWE myself, this is almost exactly my experience. Unlike you, I've only professionally worked in enterprise development. The game dev side of things is my hobby, but my experience with it sounds pretty similar to your estimates in terms of workload reduction. As an aside, my company has forced us to integrate AI tools into our workflow, and I expect this is happening in most corporations. 

Learning to prompt, correct, and iterate on AI code is a skill in and of itself. I understand my requirements and know when the AI output violates good design principles/practices. We also have code reviews at my company, so when someone is rushing and overlooks something, a reviewer catches it.

comments.author: talrnu
comments.body:
I'm an experienced programmer and I've recently been using Claude to write some code for my Unreal project. It's powerful, I'm using it to write code that will be in the finished game. But I would waste a ton of time and money if I didn't have my programming experience because I have to constantly watch it and correct it to get it to create the right thing without tying itself in knots. In its current state, I cannot imagine a non-programmer being able to make even a vertical slice or art demo game by "vibe coding" as they call it when you use AI to program without touching the code yourself. In fact I lean heavily on my experience just to make sure I'm writing prompts in a way that won't confuse it or make it do a ton of stuff I don't need.

You'll save yourself a lot of time, money, and headache just finding a human to help you make minimal games to demo your art. Even if you need to pay the programmer that helps you, it'll be worth it - though you may be able to work the angle of allowing them to use the project as a portfolio piece like you are instead of payment.

replies.author: talrnu
replies.body:
That's understandable, game jams are very likely to blow up especially if nobody involved has the experience to keep the project scope under control.

An AI won't give you a more capable programmer, but it will at least give you a programmer who's willing to do everything you say and stay completely focused on your project for as long as you want. They will misunderstand you a lot, and they'll get more and more easily confused as your project goes on. You'll need a good way to undo their work - save a separate copy of the project before you ask it to do something new, so you can delete whatever they do next if it's too broken. It's a really good idea to learn how to use version control if you don't already (both for this project and as a skill the industry requires), because that can make undoing changes a lot easier.

If that doesn't work out, just keep looking for programmers. You will eventually find one you can work with. Keep trying to do game jams, even if you don't complete the game in time to submit for the jam you can still continue working on it together to produce a portfolio piece.

comments.author: VSorceress
comments.body:
I’m not building a traditional video game, but my current project is an AI powered roleplay performance engine for interactive, adult storytelling. Right now, I’m focused on prototyping the performance engine, world building, and the narrative logic framework. The idea is to let users interact with dynamic AI personas in highly immersive RP scenarios.

I’m considering adding more explicit RPG elements as the project grows: spell casting systems, risk and failure logic, consequences, and stat or skill tracking are all on the table. The goal is to make the experience feel more game-like and less like a static story.

**Background:**  
I’m a data integration engineer by trade, so my approach is all about systems and process. Most of my experience is in building and tweaking data pipelines, logic engines, and integration workflows. This is my first deep dive into game and narrative system design. My technical skills help a lot, but the creative side (prompt engineering, story logic, character development) has definitely been a learning curve (and one I enjoy in this journey).

I also collaborate with a creative partner who co-authors the storyboarding and worldbuilding with me. We’re both longtime gamers and unapologetic book nerds, so our approach to narrative design is rooted in a deep appreciation for story, character, and immersive worlds. She’s an experienced writer with years of storytelling behind her, and is deeply involved in live, text-based roleplay across various online communities, especially in immersive, story-driven Discord groups. Her experience with character arcs, worldbuilding, and interactive story dynamics brings a lot of depth to the project and balances my technical focus. Together, we flesh out the world and narrative, then layer AI systems over it.

**What’s Working:**  
Prototyping with AI like ChatGPT and other LLMs speeds up the process of building branching narratives. It’s much faster than hand coding every path. World building is easier since I can model complex lore and have AI adapt dynamically to user input. The engine tracks user decisions and mood, which feeds into more realistic and escalating AI responses.

**What’s a Pain:**  
Context limits are a real problem. Long form, multi session scenes quickly eat up available context, so maintaining continuity is tricky. The AI can fabricate logic or rules if left to its own devices, which means I have to constantly check its work. Hosted LLMs struggle with mature content, and local models give more control but less capability. There’s no real debugger, so troubleshooting is trial and error, a lot of edge case poking, and reverse engineering logic to comply with moderation policies.

**Hybrid Logic Approach:**  
To help with hallucinations and logic drift, I’m using a hybrid approach. AI handles the creative and narrative parts, while deterministic logic (database tables and explicit rules) manage critical mechanics. The AI generates immersive scenes and dialogue but pulls outcome data or rule results directly from structured tables, not just its own context. So far, this has improved consistency for things like skill checks, branching paths, and world state management.

It’s not a classic video game, more like interactive fiction, but as I said, I’ll likely be adding RPG mechanics in the near future. If anyone else is merging AI and interactive storytelling, or coming from a non-dev background, I’m open to talking shop or swapping war stories.

replies.author: VSorceress
replies.body:
**TLDR – Core Skills and Concepts to Build AI-Powered Games/Projects:**

* TL;DR – Core Skills and Concepts to Build AI-Powered Games/Projects.
* Learn the basics of Natural Language Processing (NLP) for writing clear AI prompts.
* Practice prompt engineering. Be specific, set boundaries, double-check AI outputs.
* Pick up some basic programming (JavaScript, Python) for troubleshooting and integrating logic.
* Understand how APIs work and how to use integration platforms (Zapier, Make, Boomi, etc.)
* Focus on how to connect different tools and automate workflows, not just on the AI itself.
* Be ready to combine creative thinking, technical problem-solving, and continuous learning.

comments.author: SelfAwareWorkerDrone
comments.body:
I’m using Gemini to create Deep Research reports and podcasts based on said reports to supplement my reading of a book on the history of computers.

It failed to generate my podcast on the topic of the game Spacewar! (1962) and I started playing with the UI and there’s a new thing where it will make a web app for you if you give it a one sentence prompt.

I asked it to clone Spacewar! And it made a playable game with 2 players (P1 on WASD and P2 on the arrows on the same keyboard). It had the gravity well and physics and it worked really well; like I’d downloaded it from some classic arcade games collection.

If I were so inclined I could go through the code and ask it all kinds of questions about design patterns, how certain aspects would parallel a 2D game for production, to outline a course for me, etc.

I’d imagine you could also use it to prototype a game and then walk you through porting it to Unity, Godot, or Unreal.

People underestimate AI’s ability to be a mentor and an employee at the same time.

comments.author: AuGKlasD
comments.body:
My experience has been that AI is best used as a specialized assistant rather than a general programmer. For example, GitHub Copilot is great for writing boilerplate code or translating a chunk of logic into a language I'm less familiar with, but I wouldn't trust it to architect a whole system.

Where it's been really interesting is in the prototyping phase. I've been testing some of the prompt-based game creation platforms. A tool like MakeGamesWithAI lets you generate a simple, playable game in a minute just to see if a core idea is fun. It's a completely different workflow, more for designers or people who want to test an idea without setting up a whole project. It definitely has its limits, but for pure speed-of-thought-to-prototype, it's a fascinating new tool to have in the toolbox.
